transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-07-22 14:05 PDT | Duration: ~62 min | Recording: yes
Attendees: Miguel (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Tom (Redwood SA), Laura (CTO Kepler), Devon (SRE), Omar (ML Eng), Nina (Compliance)

[00:00] Miguel: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick agenda — priya will walk the geo routing + failover architecture, then we'll run through a couple of failure scenarios and the playbook. any additions?
[00:15] Laura: nope that sounds good, main thing for us is making sure any cross-region failover doesn't break PHI residency, so we need to call out data residency checks and private deployment considerations.
[00:28] Priya: totally. i'll flag the residency checks in the routing policy. high-level: we prefer region-local serving, but we have prioritized fallback tiers — same region different availability zone, then secondary region under restricted SSO and audit logging.
[00:45] Devon: uh can you expand on the KV cache semantics if we redirect to another region? our models rely heavily on prefix caching, cache warming is a big concern.
[00:58] Priya: sure — so two patterns we recommend: synchronous replication of hot keys for very low latency critical routes (expensive) or async warmers + optimistic miss-handling. tradeoffs: sync replication increases tail lat but keeps hit-rate; async yields cold starts but cheaper. also note that we can leverage sticky routing for short-lived sessions to keep KV local.
[01:20] Omar: how does that interact with batching? if we stick to a region for a session, batching efficiency goes up, right?
[01:30] Tom: yes, session stickiness boosts batching density. but when you failover and sessions rebalance you can see temporary throughput drop because batch windows are different. we recommend adaptive batching windows and fast-cache warmers in the new region to mitigate the throughput dip.
[01:55] Laura: compliance — nina here — if we replicate keys across region, do we get audit trails and KMS separation?
[02:05] Nina: and what about encryption at rest when we move keys?
[02:10] Priya: good call — for private deployments we keep KMS in-customer control; logs for cross-region ops are written to the customer's audit cluster, and any replication can be scoped to exclude PHI. we usually encode that as a per-route policy: residency_strict, residency_warn, residency_relaxed.
[02:35] Devon: example scenario — primary region suffers GPU exhaustion (spike from scheduling) and Dedicated pool hits queue. what's the automatic behavior?
[02:45] Priya: Redwood's smart router measures node-level queue depth, tail lat, and national-level capacity score. policy can say: on sustained p50 > X ms or queue depth > Y for Z seconds, promote region-fallback to the next priority. fallback decisions are made with hysteresis to avoid flapping.
[03:05] Miguel: we should also surface the cost signal — devon, you may prefer we failover to a cheaper quantized variant first rather than cross-region, to keep data in the same geography.
[03:15] Devon: yeah that would be ideal — send to an int8 quantized model locally before touching another jurisdiction. what's the perf delta?
[03:25] Priya: typical p95 uplift is 5–20% depending on model; tokens-per-second often improves because smaller kernels fit better in GPU caches. quality drop depends on model and prompt; we recommend per-prompt evals.
[03:40] Omar: do you have an automated rollback if quality metrics drop after fallover?
[03:48] Priya: yes — we tie quality monitors to the rollout. if the model variant shows regression on sampled prompts or evals exceed thresholds, the router can revert to a safe fallback or requeue to original region. note: there is a tradeoff window where you'll see higher latency while we route back.
[04:05] Laura: what's the operator experience for an SRE to trigger a manual failover?
[04:12] Tom: we provide runbook CLI + Console action. Console shows health map, routing topology, and one-click failover with pre-flight checks. CLI has a dry-run flag to simulate.
[04:25] Devon: we need a playbook example — stepwise, who paged, who runs the CLI, what metrics to look at.
[04:33] Miguel: priya, can you talk us through the playbook you proposed?
[04:40] Priya: sure — rough steps: detection (alert), triage (check queue depth, batch rates, KV hit-rate), mitigation 1: attempt local mitigation (scale pool, promote pre-warmed instances), mitigation 2: fall back to quantized local variant, mitigation 3: fallback to secondary region with route-scoping and audit logging. final: post-incident wrap-up and token-level cost analysis. each step has thresholds and owners in the playbook doc.
[05:10] Omar: on the KV cache warmers — can you elaborate how warmers are implemented? we have session-specific prefixes that take ~30s to warm.
[05:20] Priya: warmers are small background requests that replay typical prefixes; we provide a warm-up API and also event-driven warms on failover — when a session is attached to new region, the controller enqueues key warmers based on probability distribution. warmers are prioritized by session criticality.
[05:40] Devon: any risk of creating a DDoS pattern with warmers if many sessions failover simultaneously?
[05:48] Priya: yes which is why we have a rate-limiter and backoff. the playbook recommends phased warmers and batch windows so we don't overwhelm the target pool.
[06:00] Laura: let's talk about control-plane partitions — what if our control-plane loses visibility to a region but compute is healthy?
[06:10] Tom: we support both centralized control-plane and a private control-plane option. for control-plane partition we recommend local route caches and pre-configured static fail-overs; the nodes can continue serving with last-known-good policies and then reconcile. important to set TTLs for policy changes so stale policies don't persist.
[06:35] Omar: this sounds similar to how kubernetes handles leader partitions but focused on routing. any gotchas with version drift between policies?
[06:45] Priya: yes — we recommend policy version pinning and a reconcile hook that enforces compatibility; when a node rejoins, it validates checksums. we log mismatch events to the audit trail.
[07:00] Devon: can you quantify expected latency blips when failing over to secondary region? our SLO is p99 < 300ms for user-facing inference.
[07:12] Priya: from our internal tests: cold failover (no warmers, different region) p99 can jump 2–3x for several minutes while caches warm. with sticky sessions and pre-warmers the blip is usually contained to 10–30s and p99 increases by ~10–40% depending on distance and peering. if you choose local quantized variant instead, the increase is much smaller but quality needs to be validated.
[07:45] Laura: and network egress costs? moving to another region will incur egress fees — can Redwood surface cost estimates pre-failover?
[07:55] Miguel: yes we can estimate egress + token costs and show a delta in the console; that will be part of the runbook decision matrix.
[08:05] Devon: about VPC/on-prem — if we go private in our VPC, do you still do smart routing across our internal regions?
[08:14] Tom: for private deployments we deploy regional control-plane agents into your VPCs. routing decisions can be made locally; cross-region routing requires VPN/peering and explicit config. the difference is you control network and KMS.
[08:30] Omar: for on-prem we might not have GPUs in every region — can Redwood route to cloud-hosted Dedicated pools while keeping audit logs in our VPC?
[08:42] Priya: yes, hybrid mode: compute can be hosted while control and logs remain in customer VPC. we have secure egress tunnels and token scoping so that PHI never leaves controlled channels.
[08:55] Laura: okay let's sketch a concrete policy for us: prefer same-region non-quantized; if p95 > 150ms for 2 minutes, try local quantized; if p95 > 300ms for 1 minute after that, failover to secondary region with audit logging and sandboxed KMS. does that sound feasible?
[09:12] Priya: yes that's implementable. we'll encode thresholds and hysteresis. also recommend a canary flow: send 5% of traffic to secondary region first and monitor quality delta before full shift.
[09:30] Miguel: question on benchmarking — we should run a mixed workload that mimics Kepler's bursty overnight jobs plus daytime interactive requests. priya, can you lead the bench design?
[09:38] Priya: yes — will propose load shapes, and we want Omar's real prompt sets to get realistic KV-hit distributions.
[09:45] Omar: i'll share token distribution and a 24-hour sample.
[09:50] Nina: compliance note — any cross-region transfer must be logged with user-id and purpose; we need a proving artifact for audits.
[10:00] Tom: audit hooks are generated with every route decision — we can attach request-level metadata and ship to your SIEM.
[10:08] Devon: concerned about control-plane remote exec — does Redwood require inbound access to our infra for private deployments?
[10:18] Miguel: no inbound; we run connectors outbound from customer network. for on-prem we can provide an air-gapped package and offline keys.
[10:28] Laura: this is helpful. can we go through two failure scenarios quickly?
[10:33] Priya: scenario A: AZ-level outage in us-west-2 while compute in us-west-2 remains reachable but under-provisioned. Steps: detection (queue spikes), mitigate (scale local Dedicated pool), if unsuccessful: route 20% to quantized local, monitor quality, then escalate to failover to us-east-1 with canary 5% then full shift. Post-incident: analyze token-cost delta, KV-hit drop graphs, and plan warmers.
[11:00] Priya: scenario B: control-plane partition to eu-west-1; compute healthy. local agents switch to cached policies, serve read-only; SRE runs dry-run failover if desired; once control-plane resumes, reconcile policies and surface policy drift alerts.
[11:22] Omar: for scenario A, what's the expected cache hit-rate drop?
[11:28] Priya: depends, but for session-heavy workloads we see 40–70% drop initially then recover to 85% after warmers in ~2–6 minutes based on batch windows.
[11:45] Miguel: ok let's capture the follow-ups — priya will produce the playbook draft and bench plan; miguel will send pricing; omar/devon provide dataset and SRE constraints.
[11:58] Laura: thank you all. we also want a one-page summary of the failover policy that we can show execs.
[12:05] Miguel: will do, one-pager added to next steps.
[12:10] Meeting end.
